headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Postpartum Care
headings.content: Postpartum care, also known as postnatal care, is a critical phase in maternal and child health that begins immediately after the delivery of the placenta and extends through the first six weeks, or 42 days, following childbirth. This period is often referred to as the puerperium. During this transitional phase, the mother's body undergoes profound anatomical, physiological, and psychological changes as it returns to the pre-pregnant state. For nursing students in Nigeria, understanding postpartum care is essential because maternal mortality and morbidity remain significant public health challenges in the region. Effective postpartum care aims to monitor the mother for potential complications such as postpartum hemorrhage and puerperal sepsis, support successful breastfeeding, promote emotional well-being, and provide education on newborn care and contraception. Nurses serve as the primary educators and advocates for postpartum mothers, ensuring that both mother and baby receive holistic, evidence-based care whether in a primary health center, general hospital, or during community health extension visits. By providing structured assessment, timely intervention, and empathetic support, nurses can significantly reduce maternal and neonatal mortality rates and foster healthy family dynamics during this vulnerable period.

headings.title: Immediate Postpartum Physiological Changes and Involution
headings.content: Following delivery, the maternal body initiates a series of rapid physiological adaptations known collectively as involution, whereby the reproductive organs, particularly the uterus, return to their non-pregnant size and condition. Involution is driven by the abrupt withdrawal of placental hormones like estrogen and progesterone, combined with sustained oxytocin release stimulated by uterine contractions and breastfeeding. Immediately after the third stage of labor, the uterus should feel firm, globular, and palpable roughly at the level of the umbilicus or slightly below. Over the next two weeks, the uterus descends into the true pelvis at a rate of approximately one centimeter or one fingerbreadth per day, becoming non-palpable abdominally by day ten to fourteen. Concurrently, lochia—the postpartum uterine discharge—evolves in color and consistency. It begins as lochia rubra (red and bloody for the first 1 to 3 days), transitions to lochia serosa (pinkish-brown from day 4 to 10), and finally becomes lochia alba (yellowish-white from day 10 to 6 weeks). Nurses must regularly assess uterine tone and lochia characteristics to detect subinvolution or hemorrhage early. Other physiological changes include postpartum diuresis to eliminate excess extracellular fluid accumulated during pregnancy, and rapid blood volume adjustments as uteroplacental circulation ceases.

headings.title: Comprehensive Maternal Assessment in the Puerperium
headings.content: A comprehensive maternal assessment during the puerperium is vital for detecting early signs of physical deviation or complications. Standardized clinical evaluations often follow the acronym BUBBLE-EE, which stands for Breasts, Uterus, Bowel, Bladder, Lochia, Episiotomy/Perineum, Emotional status, and Extremities (for thromboembolism risk). The nurse begins by examining the breasts for engorgement, nipple integrity, and readiness for lactation. The uterine fundus is palpated to ensure it remains firmly contracted; a boggy or relaxed uterus indicates uterine atony and impending hemorrhage. Bowel sounds and history of flatus passage are checked to rule out constipation or ileus, especially after cesarean sections. Bladder assessment involves monitoring for adequate voiding and urinary retention, which can displace the uterus and worsen bleeding. The character, amount, and odor of lochia are meticulously documented. The perineum is inspected for edema, hematomas, bruising, and the integrity of episiotomy or tear repairs using the REEDA scale (Redness, Edema, Ecchymosis, Discharge, Approximation). Assessment of emotional status helps identify blues or depression, while inspecting the lower extremities for unilateral swelling, warmth, and pain helps rule out deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

headings.title: Routine Postpartum Nursing Interventions and Comfort Measures
headings.content: Routine nursing interventions in the postpartum ward focus on promoting comfort, preventing infection, and facilitating physical recovery. Following vaginal delivery, perineal discomfort from lacerations or episiotomies is common and can be managed effectively with non-pharmacological comfort measures. Nurses should instruct mothers to apply cold packs or ice compresses to the perineum during the first 24 hours to minimize edema and numb nerve endings. After 24 hours, warm sitz baths promote vasodilation, enhance healing, and relieve local pain. Proper perineal hygiene—such as washing the area from front to back with clean water after every voiding or defecation and changing maternity pads frequently—is essential to prevent ascending puerperal infections. Pain relief analgesics, such as paracetamol or ibuprofen, should be administered as prescribed to manage afterpains (uterine contractions) and incisional pain for cesarean mothers. Early ambulation is strongly encouraged within 6 to 12 hours post-delivery to prevent venous stasis and lower extremity deep vein thrombosis, provided the patient's blood pressure and spinal anesthesia recovery permit. Additionally, nurses must ensure adequate hydration and monitor spontaneous micturition within 6 hours of delivery to prevent urinary tract infections and bladder distention.

headings.title: Nutrition, Hygiene, and Self-Care Education
headings.content: Nutritional counseling and personal hygiene education are pivotal components of holistic postpartum care, especially in resource-constrained settings where maternal depletion can occur. Lactating mothers have significantly increased metabolic demands; they require an extra 300 to 500 calories per day compared to their pre-pregnancy intake, along with adequate protein, calcium, and iron-rich foods to support milk production and replenish blood loss. In Nigeria, nurses should promote culturally acceptable, nutrient-dense local foods such as beans, lean meats, fish, leafy green vegetables, and fortified staples. Hydration is equally critical; mothers should drink water whenever they feel thirsty and maintain fluid intake during breastfeeding sessions. Regarding hygiene, daily bathing with clean water and soap is encouraged, and cultural myths advising against bathing or hair washing should be gently dispelled with health education. Hand hygiene before handling the newborn or breastfeeding prevents cross-contamination. Rest is another vital aspect of self-care; nurses must teach mothers to sleep when the baby sleeps to combat exhaustion, which is a major contributor to postpartum mood disturbances.

headings.title: Postpartum Psychological Adjustment and Mental Health Screening
headings.content: Postpartum psychological adjustment involves navigating the complex emotional and hormonal shifts that accompany childbirth. Up to 80% of women experience 'postpartum blues' within the first few days after delivery, characterized by mild mood swings, tearfulness, anxiety, and fatigue. These symptoms are transient, typically resolving within two weeks without formal psychiatric intervention, requiring primarily reassurance, rest, and family support. However, nurses must remain vigilant for more severe and persistent conditions, such as postpartum depression (PPD) and postpartum psychosis. PPD presents with intense feelings of sadness, severe mood swings, apathy toward the newborn, inability to care for oneself or the baby, and sometimes suicidal ideation, lasting beyond two weeks. Postpartum psychosis is a rare psychiatric emergency marked by hallucinations, delusions, and bizarre behavior that poses a danger to both mother and child. Routine mental health screening using validated tools like the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) should be integrated into postpartum visits. Nurses must cultivate a non-judgmental, empathetic environment that encourages mothers to express their emotional concerns without fear of stigma.

headings.title: Identification and Management of Postpartum Complications
headings.content: Prompt identification and management of postpartum complications are crucial for reducing maternal morbidity and mortality. Primary postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), defined as blood loss exceeding 500 mL after vaginal delivery or 1000 mL after cesarean section within 24 hours, is most commonly caused by uterine atony. Secondary PPH occurs between 24 hours and 12 weeks postpartum, often due to retained placental fragments or subinvolution. Nurses must monitor vital signs meticulously, watch for tachycardia and hypotension, and quantify blood loss accurately. Immediate nursing actions for PPH include calling for help, massaging the boggy uterus, administering uterotonic drugs (such as oxytocin, ergometrine, or misoprostol) as prescribed, and establishing large-bore intravenous access. Another major complication is puerperal sepsis, an infection of the genital tract characterized by fever, foul-smelling lochia, and lower abdominal pain, which requires prompt antibiotic therapy. Thromboembolic disorders, mastitis, and urinary tract infections also require vigilant monitoring and timely medical intervention to prevent systemic deterioration.

headings.title: Neonatal Transition Support and Breastfeeding Guidance
headings.content: Supporting neonatal transition and providing expert breastfeeding guidance are core responsibilities of the postpartum nurse. Immediate neonatal care involves establishing and maintaining airway patency, ensuring thermal regulation through skin-to-skin contact, and initiating early breastfeeding within the first hour of life. Skin-to-skin contact stabilizes the newborn's heart rate, blood pressure, and body temperature while promoting maternal-infant bonding and milk let-down. Nurses play a crucial role in supporting exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life, as recommended by the World Health Organization. Education should cover correct positioning and attachment (latch-on) techniques to prevent common complications like sore, cracked nipples and breast engorgement. Mothers must understand the importance of feeding on demand (both day and night) and recognizing hunger cues such as rooting, sucking motions, and stirring. The nurse should also teach mothers how to assess adequate infant hydration and milk transfer by monitoring wet diapers (at least 6 wet diapers per day by day five) and adequate weight gain. Addressing challenges early prevents premature cessation of breastfeeding and ensures optimal infant nutrition.

headings.title: Family Planning and Postpartum Discharge Counseling
headings.content: Family planning education and comprehensive postpartum discharge counseling empower mothers to make informed decisions regarding their reproductive health and future pregnancies. Return of fertility can occur before the resumption of menstruation, particularly in non-breastfeeding mothers, making contraceptive counseling an essential part of postpartum care before hospital discharge. Nurses must discuss various family planning options tailored to individual client needs and medical history, including barrier methods, long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARCs) like intrauterine devices (IUDs) and implants, injectables, and progestin-only pills (which do not interfere with lactation). Combined hormonal contraceptives are generally avoided during the first few weeks postpartum, especially in breastfeeding mothers, due to the increased risk of venous thromboembolism and potential reduction in milk supply. Discharge counseling should also review danger signs that require immediate return to the healthcare facility—such as heavy vaginal bleeding, severe headache, visual disturbances, chest pain, calf swelling, and fever. Finally, nurses must confirm that follow-up appointments (such as the 6-week postnatal checkup) are scheduled, ensuring continuity of care and long-term maternal well-being.
